cards.definition: Conditional probability P(A|B) is P(A intersect B)/P(B) when P(B)>0. It measures probability within the information or restriction represented by B, not a claim that B causes A.
major_error_concepts: Interchanging P(A|B) and P(B|A) without justification.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Probability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Joint probability divided by positive conditioning probability.
Conditioning differs from causation.

cards.definition: A joint distribution describes probabilities or densities for several random quantities together. It determines dependence structure as well as the individual marginal distributions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming marginal distributions alone uniquely determine the joint distribution.
cards.prompt: What is Joint Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distribution of quantities considered together.

accepted_variants: Elimination of nuisance variables by probability integration.
cards.definition: Marginalization obtains a distribution for selected variables by summing or integrating a joint distribution over the others. Integrating out uncertainty differs from fixing variables at estimates.
major_error_concepts: Calling replacement by a mean value marginalization.
cards.prompt: What is Marginalization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sum or integrate over omitted variables.
Not plug-in substitution.

accepted_variants: Independence after conditioning on specified information.
cards.definition: Conditional independence means the joint conditional law factors given the conditioning information. Variables can be dependent marginally yet independent conditional on a common parameter or latent variable.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the conditioning variable and assuming the independence still holds.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Independence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conditional factorization.
Does not imply unconditional independence.

cards.definition: Bayes' theorem updates a hypothesis using evidence: posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by evidence, when the evidence probability is positive. For a complete hypothesis partition, evidence is the sum of likelihood-prior products.
major_error_concepts: Reporting P(D|H) itself as the posterior without prior or normalization.
cards.prompt: What is Bayes' Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct posterior normalization.
Positive evidence and complete alternative accounting.

cards.definition: A statistical model is a family of probability distributions for observations indexed by parameters and assumptions. Bayesian analysis adds a prior law to this sampling model rather than replacing the observation model.
major_error_concepts: Treating a prior alone as a complete model of observed data.
cards.prompt: What is Statistical Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distribution family for observations.
Separate sampling model and prior.

accepted_variants: The model's unknown state or coefficient.
cards.definition: A parameter is an unknown quantity indexing a statistical model, while the parameter space is the set of allowed values. Bayesian uncertainty assigns a distribution over that space within the chosen model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all parameters may take arbitrary real values regardless of model constraints.
cards.prompt: What is Parameter and Parameter Space? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unknown model-indexing quantity with a specified allowed space.

cards.definition: A likelihood is the observation model evaluated at the observed data and viewed as a function of parameters. It is not generally a probability density over parameters and need not integrate to one over parameter space.
major_error_concepts: Normalizing likelihood over parameters without a prior and calling that universally Bayesian updating.
cards.prompt: What is Likelihood? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Data fixed, parameters varied.
Not a normalized parameter distribution by itself.

cards.definition: A prior is a probability law on the parameter space used before conditioning on the current data. Its support, scale, propriety, and relationship to earlier information are part of the model specification.
major_error_concepts: Calling a penalty a complete prior without its probability interpretation or transformation rules.
cards.prompt: What is Prior Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Parameter probability law before current-data conditioning.
Specify support and scale.

cards.definition: A posterior is the conditional parameter distribution given the observed data under the specified likelihood and prior. It combines those assumptions and therefore is not an assumption-free probability statement.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the posterior is independent of the model assumptions used to obtain it.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Parameter law after conditioning on observations.
Depends on both likelihood and prior.

cards.definition: Model evidence is the probability or density of the observed data after integrating the likelihood over the prior. It normalizes the posterior and depends on the whole prior predictive specification.
major_error_concepts: Replacing integration over parameters with the maximum likelihood value.
cards.prompt: What is Model Evidence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Integral of likelihood times prior.
Normalizer and prior predictive data density.

cards.definition: The expression posterior proportional to likelihood times prior suppresses a normalizing factor independent of the parameters. It is useful for deriving posterior shape but does not remove the need for a finite positive normalizer.
major_error_concepts: Dropping a parameter-dependent factor as if it were constant.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Kernel? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Omitted factor must not depend on the parameter.
Normalization must exist.

cards.definition: For a prior on Euclidean parameter space, its support consists of points whose every open neighborhood has positive prior probability. This is not the set of points with positive singleton probability or the positive set of one arbitrary density version. In ordinary likelihood-weighted updating with a finite positive normalizer, every prior-null measurable set remains posterior-null. In particular, a whole neighborhood excluded by the prior cannot be restored by that update.
major_error_concepts: A uniform prior on [0,1] excludes 0.5 from its support because P(theta=0.5)=0.
cards.prompt: What is prior support for a continuous parameter, and what does ordinary Bayesian updating preserve about prior-null regions?
required_concepts: Use positive probability in every neighborhood to characterize support.
Do not interpret zero point probability in a continuous prior as exclusion from support.
Under a finite-positive-normalizer likelihood update, prior-null regions stay posterior-null.

accepted_variants: A prior with total probability one.
cards.definition: A proper prior integrates or sums to one over its parameter space. Proper priors are especially important for well-defined prior predictive distributions and conventional model-evidence calculations.
major_error_concepts: Equating a broad proper prior with an improper flat measure.
cards.prompt: What is Proper Prior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normalized probability law.

cards.definition: An improper prior is a prior-like nonnegative measure with infinite total mass, so no finite positive normalizing constant turns it into a probability law. This differs from a proper prior written as an unnormalized kernel with a finite positive integral. An improper prior can sometimes produce a proper posterior, but posterior propriety must be checked, and its arbitrary multiplicative constant generally prevents ordinary model-evidence comparison.
major_error_concepts: The kernel exp(-theta^2/2) is an improper prior because its normalizing constant has not yet been written.
cards.prompt: Distinguish an improper prior from a proper prior written only up to a normalizing constant.
required_concepts: Infinite prior mass is not normalizable; merely suppressing a finite normalizer is different.
A proper posterior is possible but not guaranteed.
Arbitrary improper-prior constants cannot be used naively as model evidence.

accepted_variants: Existence of a normalized posterior law.
cards.definition: Posterior propriety means the likelihood-prior kernel has a finite positive integral so it defines a probability distribution. This must be established separately when an improper prior or weakly identified model is used.
major_error_concepts: Treating a sampler's numerical output as proof that the posterior is proper.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Propriety? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Finite positive posterior normalizing constant.

cards.definition: The prior predictive distribution averages the observation model over the prior before current data are observed. It reveals what kinds of data the combined model predicts a priori.
major_error_concepts: Checking only the prior's parameter plot while ignoring its implied data scale and calling that a prior predictive check.
cards.prompt: What is Prior Predictive Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Integrate sampling distribution over prior.

cards.definition: The posterior predictive law is p(y_new|y)=integral p(y_new|theta,y) p(theta|y) dtheta, with a sum for discrete parameters. When future and observed data are conditionally independent given theta, the first factor becomes p(y_new|theta). This mixture generally differs from a plug-in law, but a shortcut is valid when it equals the mixture: one future Bernoulli outcome has predictive success probability E[theta|y]. Multiple future outcomes can remain predictively dependent through the shared uncertain parameter.
major_error_concepts: For any posterior over theta, two future conditionally independent Bernoulli outcomes are marginally independent Bernoulli(E[theta|y]).
cards.prompt: Define the posterior predictive distribution and explain when a plug-in expression can or cannot equal it.
required_concepts: Average the appropriate future-data law over the posterior.
Use conditional independence only when it belongs to the model.
Distinguish a generally unjustified plug-in substitution from a demonstrated exact special case.

cards.definition: A plug-in prediction uses one parameter estimate in the observation model. It can be useful but usually omits uncertainty from the remaining parameter distribution unless that uncertainty is incorporated separately.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a plug-in predictive interval automatically includes all parameter uncertainty.
cards.prompt: What is Plug-In Prediction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Replace parameter uncertainty with a single estimate.
Distinguish from full posterior integration.

cards.definition: Sequential Bayesian updating uses a previous posterior as the prior for new evidence, with the new likelihood conditional on information already used. Reusing the same observations as independent new evidence double-counts them.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying by the same data likelihood repeatedly and calling each multiplication fresh evidence.
cards.prompt: What is Sequential Updating? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Posterior becomes next prior with correctly conditioned new evidence.
Avoid double counting.

cards.definition: For two hypotheses, posterior odds equal prior odds times the likelihood ratio for the observed evidence. The likelihood ratio measures evidence between hypotheses, not posterior probability by itself.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a likelihood ratio of ten as posterior probability ten or certainty without prior odds.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Odds? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Posterior odds = prior odds times evidence ratio.

cards.definition: A Bayes factor is the ratio of two models' marginal likelihoods for the same observed data. It updates prior model odds into posterior odds and depends on each model's prior predictive distribution.
major_error_concepts: Replacing marginal likelihoods by maximized likelihoods and calling the ratio a Bayes factor.
cards.prompt: What is Bayes Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Evidence ratio between fully specified models.
Parameter priors affect the factor.

cards.definition: A prior family is conjugate to a likelihood when updating leaves the posterior in the same distribution family. Conjugacy simplifies computation but does not guarantee that the family is appropriate for the application.
major_error_concepts: Assuming conjugate means objectively correct or data-independent.
cards.prompt: What is Conjugate Prior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Prior and posterior share a family under the specified likelihood.

accepted_variants: A two-shape-parameter prior for a Bernoulli probability.
cards.definition: The beta distribution is a flexible distribution on a probability parameter between zero and one, with positive shape parameters alpha and beta. Its density is proportional to theta^(alpha-1)(1-theta)^(beta-1).
major_error_concepts: Allowing a beta-distributed probability outside zero to one.
cards.prompt: What is Beta Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Support on probability values.
Positive shape parameters and kernel.

cards.definition: With a Beta(alpha,beta) prior and a binomial sample containing s successes and f failures, the posterior is Beta(alpha+s,beta+f). The update assumes the stated common success probability and sampling model.
major_error_concepts: Adding the total sample size to both shape parameters.
cards.prompt: What is Beta–Binomial Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Add successes and failures to the corresponding shapes.

cards.definition: In the shape-rate convention, Gamma(alpha,beta) has density f(x)=beta^alpha x^(alpha-1) exp(-beta x)/Gamma(alpha) for x>0, with alpha>0 and beta>0. In a shape-scale convention s=1/beta, the same density is x^(alpha-1)exp(-x/s)/(Gamma(alpha)s^alpha). The value assigned to the density at a single boundary point does not change the law.
major_error_concepts: Gamma(alpha,beta) in the shape-rate convention has density proportional to x^(alpha-1)exp(-x/beta).
cards.prompt: State the Gamma density using a declared shape-rate or shape-scale convention.
required_concepts: State a correct Gamma density with positive shape and rate or scale.
Rate and scale are reciprocals, not interchangeable symbols.
The variable is positive.

cards.definition: A gamma prior is conjugate to a Poisson rate. In the shape-rate convention, observed counts add to the shape and total exposure adds to the rate, with exposure units matched to the Poisson model.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring differing observation exposures when updating the rate.
cards.prompt: What is Gamma–Poisson Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Counts update shape; exposure updates rate.
Declare gamma parameterization.

cards.definition: Let Y_1,...,Y_n be conditionally iid N(mu,sigma^2), with known sigma^2>0, and let mu have prior N(m_0,tau_0^2), tau_0^2>0. Then mu|y is N(m_n,tau_n^2), where tau_n^2=(1/tau_0^2+n/sigma^2)^(-1) and m_n=tau_n^2(m_0/tau_0^2+n*ybar/sigma^2). Prior precision and sample-mean precision add; correlated observations require their actual joint likelihood rather than blindly using n/sigma^2.
major_error_concepts: The posterior variance is tau_0^2+sigma^2/n, and the noisier mean gets the larger weight.
cards.prompt: Give the posterior mean and variance for a normal prior on the mean of conditionally iid normal observations with known variance.
required_concepts: State the conditionally iid known-variance model and normal prior.
Give the posterior precision 1/tau_0^2+n/sigma^2.
Give its corresponding precision-weighted mean.

cards.definition: When both a normal mean and variance are unknown, joint prior choices such as normal-inverse-gamma support conjugate analysis. Marginalizing variance can produce Student-t uncertainty for the mean or future observations under the standard model.
major_error_concepts: Treating estimated variance as known without acknowledging lost uncertainty.
cards.prompt: What is Normal Model with Unknown Variance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Joint uncertainty in mean and variance.
Integrating variance changes the marginal distribution.

cards.definition: For K≥2 and alpha_i>0, Dirichlet(alpha_1,...,alpha_K) has density Gamma(alpha_0)/product_i Gamma(alpha_i) times product_i theta_i^(alpha_i-1), where alpha_0=sum_i alpha_i. The density is with respect to the first K-1 simplex coordinates, theta_i>0 and sum_i theta_i=1. Its coordinate mean is E[theta_i]=alpha_i/alpha_0. The coordinates are constrained, not independent probability parameters.
major_error_concepts: The Dirichlet law consists of independent Gamma coordinates used directly as probabilities without normalization.
cards.prompt: State the Dirichlet density, parameter restrictions, and mean proportions.
required_concepts: Give the simplex density or its kernel with an explicitly stated normalizer.
All concentration parameters are positive and coordinates sum to one.
The mean coordinate is alpha_i divided by total concentration.

cards.definition: For categorical counts with a Dirichlet prior, the posterior concentration for each category is its prior parameter plus that category's count. All categories share the normalization through the total concentration.
major_error_concepts: Normalizing each category independently without enforcing total probability one.
cards.prompt: What is Dirichlet–Multinomial Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Add category counts to prior concentrations.

accepted_variants: A statistic through which the data's parameter dependence factors.
cards.definition: A sufficient statistic retains all sample information about the parameter within a specified likelihood model. Bayesian updating can then use its parameter-dependent likelihood contribution without preserving irrelevant sample details for that parameter inference.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a statistic sufficient for one model is sufficient after changing the observation model.
cards.prompt: What is Sufficient Statistic? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sufficiency is relative to a statistical model and parameter.

cards.definition: A standard common-support exponential family has density p_theta(x)=h(x) exp(eta(theta)^T T(x)-A(eta(theta))) with respect to a fixed dominating measure. Here h and T do not depend on theta, eta is the natural parameter, and A(eta)=log integral h(x)exp(eta^T T(x)) dx on the domain where that integral is finite and positive. The vector statistic T carries the displayed parameter dependence; merely containing an exponential symbol is insufficient.
major_error_concepts: A density is in this common-support exponential-family form whenever it contains exp(theta*x), even if the remaining support indicator depends arbitrarily on theta.
cards.prompt: State the standard common-support exponential-family density and identify its natural parameter, statistic, and log normalizer.
required_concepts: Give h(x)exp(eta(theta)^T T(x)-A(eta(theta))).
h and T are parameter-independent under a fixed dominating measure and common-support convention.
A normalizes the density on its admissible natural-parameter domain.

cards.definition: A credible interval is a parameter interval containing a specified posterior probability under the model. It describes conditional uncertainty after observing data, unlike a confidence procedure's repeated-sampling coverage definition.
major_error_concepts: Defining a 95 percent credible interval solely by repeated-sampling coverage over hypothetical datasets.
cards.prompt: What is Credible Interval? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Specified posterior mass conditional on data and model.

cards.definition: For 0<alpha<1, let q_p=inf{x:F(x)≥p} be a posterior quantile. The central quantile interval [q_(alpha/2),q_(1-alpha/2)] leaves tail probabilities alpha/2 each for a continuous posterior. With atoms, each excluded tail is at most alpha/2 and the interval can contain more than 1-alpha posterior mass; exact equal tails may be impossible without randomization. It need not be a shortest credible interval.
major_error_concepts: A posterior putting probability 0.99 at zero always has a nonrandomized 95 percent interval with exactly 2.5 percent mass in each excluded tail.
cards.prompt: Define an equal-tailed posterior interval using quantiles and explain the caveat for a discrete posterior.
required_concepts: Use the alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2 posterior quantiles.
Exact equal tails apply in the continuous case; atoms can force unequal smaller tails and excess coverage.
Do not claim minimum length in general.

cards.definition: For a continuous posterior density p in fixed coordinates, an HPD region of mass 1-alpha includes all points with p(theta)>c and, when needed, a suitable part of the level set p(theta)=c so its total posterior mass is 1-alpha. Points included at the boundary have no lower density than points excluded, apart from null-set conventions. Ties can make the region nonunique; multimodality can make it disconnected, and nonlinear reparameterization can change it.
major_error_concepts: Under a uniform posterior on [0,1], a 95 percent HPD region cannot exist because every strict density threshold contains either none or all of the probability.
cards.prompt: Define a continuous-posterior HPD region, including how density ties affect the construction.
required_concepts: Select highest-density points to the target mass, allowing selection within a tied density level.
Density plateaus can make the answer nonunique.
Disconnected regions and coordinate dependence are allowed.

cards.definition: The posterior mean is m=E[theta|y], finite when E[|theta||y]<infinity. If E[theta^2|y]<infinity, posterior squared-error risk decomposes as E[(theta-a)^2|y]=Var(theta|y)+(a-m)^2, so the unique minimizing scalar action is a=m. A finite mean with infinite second moment does not supply a finite squared-error risk: every finite action then has infinite expected squared loss.
major_error_concepts: Whenever the posterior mean exists, choosing it makes expected squared-error loss finite even if the posterior has infinite variance.
cards.prompt: Define the posterior mean and state when it is the unique finite-risk squared-error Bayes action.
required_concepts: Distinguish existence of the posterior mean from existence of finite squared-error risk.
With a finite second moment, use the variance-plus-squared-distance decomposition to identify the minimizer.

cards.definition: A posterior median divides posterior probability so that at least half lies on each side. It is a minimizer of posterior expected absolute-error loss for the scalar estimation problem under the relevant existence conditions.
major_error_concepts: Equating median with mean in every skewed posterior.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Median? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Posterior halfway probability point.
Absolute-loss optimality.

cards.definition: A maximum a posteriori estimate is a maximizer of posterior density in a specified parameterization. It is a point summary, can be nonunique, and does not characterize posterior uncertainty by itself.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the MAP is invariant under every nonlinear reparameterization.
cards.prompt: What is Maximum a Posteriori Estimate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Posterior density mode in stated coordinates.
Not a full uncertainty description.

accepted_variants: A change of variables on parameter space.
cards.definition: Reparameterization describes the same model through transformed coordinates. Probabilities of corresponding events remain consistent, but densities change with the Jacobian and density-based modes can move.
major_error_concepts: Keeping the same numeric density under a nonlinear coordinate change without a Jacobian.
cards.prompt: What is Reparameterization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Change parameter coordinates consistently.
Densities require a transformation factor.

cards.definition: A Jacobian factor adjusts a density under a differentiable invertible change of variables. For eta=g(theta), the new density includes the absolute determinant of the derivative of the inverse map.
major_error_concepts: Using the forward determinant when the inverse determinant is required by the displayed formula.
cards.prompt: What is Jacobian Density Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Absolute determinant of inverse transformation derivative.
Preserves integrated probabilities.

cards.definition: A loss function L(theta,a) assigns a cost to action a when the unknown state is theta. It encodes the decision objective separately from the likelihood and prior.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a posterior distribution uniquely chooses an action without any objective or loss.
cards.prompt: What is Loss Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Cost indexed by true state and chosen action.
Separate from probability assumptions.

cards.definition: Posterior expected loss averages L(theta,a) over the posterior for each candidate action after the observed data are fixed. Minimizing it chooses an action suited to both current uncertainty and the specified cost.
major_error_concepts: Averaging over hypothetical future datasets instead of the current posterior and calling it posterior expected loss.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Expected Loss? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Conditional expectation of loss over posterior states.

cards.definition: A Bayes action minimizes posterior expected loss for the observed data. Different losses can select different actions from the same posterior, so no single point summary is optimal for all decisions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the MAP estimate is the best decision under every loss.
cards.prompt: What is Bayes Action? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimize posterior expected loss.
Choice depends on loss.

cards.definition: Squared-error loss penalizes an estimation error by its square. When the relevant posterior moments exist, its expected loss is minimized by the posterior mean.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the posterior median always minimizes squared error.
cards.prompt: What is Squared-Error Loss? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Squared deviation loss.
Mean minimizes posterior squared loss.

cards.definition: Absolute-error loss penalizes the magnitude of estimation error. A posterior median minimizes its expected value in the scalar decision problem.
major_error_concepts: Automatically choosing the mean as the absolute-loss minimizer for every skewed posterior.
cards.prompt: What is Absolute-Error Loss? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Absolute deviation loss.
Median is a minimizer.

cards.definition: Asymmetric loss assigns different costs to overestimation and underestimation or to different decision errors. The resulting optimal action can be a posterior quantile or probability threshold different from the symmetric-loss choice.
major_error_concepts: Using a fixed 0.5 decision threshold despite explicitly unequal error costs without justification.
cards.prompt: What is Asymmetric Loss? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Different error directions carry different costs.

accepted_variants: Posterior uncertainty translated into decision consequences.
cards.definition: Decision uncertainty concerns the possible consequences of an action under posterior uncertainty. A narrow parameter interval does not by itself imply low decision risk if the loss is highly sensitive near a boundary.
major_error_concepts: Equating a small posterior standard deviation with universally negligible expected loss.
cards.prompt: What is Uncertainty in Decisions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Assess action consequences, not parameter spread alone.

accepted_variants: Robustness analysis with respect to the prior.
cards.definition: Prior sensitivity analysis compares conclusions under substantively plausible alternative priors. It identifies which results depend strongly on prior choices rather than treating one convenient prior as assumption-free.
major_error_concepts: Changing only an irrelevant prior detail and claiming all prior sensitivity has been exhausted.
cards.prompt: What is Prior Sensitivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compare reasonable prior specifications and resulting conclusions.

cards.definition: A weakly informative prior rules out implausible scales or behaviors while leaving substantial room for the data to inform the parameters. Its informativeness is relative to the model and measurement scale.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a very wide prior is automatically weakly informative on the implied data scale.
cards.prompt: What is Weakly Informative Prior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Regularize implausible behavior without tight substantive concentration.
Scale-dependent notion.

cards.definition: An informative prior encodes meaningful existing knowledge or constraints about the parameter. Its source, applicability, and overlap with the current data should be clear to avoid hidden double use of evidence.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a prior is justified solely because it produces a desired posterior conclusion.
cards.prompt: What is Informative Prior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Substantive prior knowledge.
Avoid double counting current evidence.

cards.definition: Jeffreys prior is proportional to the square root of the Fisher-information determinant under the regular model definition. It has a useful reparameterization property but may be improper and is not a universally context-free solution to prior choice.
major_error_concepts: Assuming Jeffreys prior is always proper or automatically optimal for every decision.
cards.prompt: What is Jeffreys Prior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Square root of information determinant.
May be improper.

cards.definition: Prior scale describes the range of parameter values receiving substantial probability in meaningful units. Rescaling predictors or outcomes changes the interpretation of a numeric prior width and can require transforming the prior consistently.
major_error_concepts: Applying identical coefficient-prior numbers after arbitrary unit changes without adjusting interpretation.
cards.prompt: What is Prior Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Width interpreted in model units.
Coordinate scaling matters.

cards.definition: A hierarchical model links parameters across groups through a shared distribution with its own parameters. It represents related-but-not-identical groups and can learn the amount of cross-group pooling from data.
major_error_concepts: Assuming hierarchical means all group parameters are forced equal.
cards.prompt: What is Hierarchical Model? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Group parameters share a higher-level distribution.

cards.definition: A hyperparameter controls a prior or higher-level distribution, such as a group-effect mean or scale. It may be fixed, estimated, or assigned a hyperprior depending on the model.
major_error_concepts: Treating every hyperparameter as necessarily known exactly.
cards.prompt: What is Hyperparameter? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Parameter of a prior-level distribution.

cards.definition: A hyperprior assigns a probability distribution to a hyperparameter. This propagates uncertainty about group-level or prior-scale quantities instead of replacing them automatically with fixed estimates.
major_error_concepts: Claiming assigning a hyperprior eliminates all dependence on modeling choices.
cards.prompt: What is Hyperprior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Prior law for a higher-level parameter.

cards.definition: Exchangeability means the joint distribution is unchanged by reordering observations or groups in the specified class. It supports common hierarchical representations in appropriate settings but does not mean observed values are identical.
major_error_concepts: Assuming time series are automatically exchangeable despite temporal dependence.
cards.prompt: What is Exchangeability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Permutation-invariant joint law.
Different from equality of observations.

cards.definition: Partial pooling shares information across groups while allowing group-specific estimates. The amount of shrinkage depends on group information and the inferred between-group variation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every group is shrunk by exactly the same amount regardless of sample information.
cards.prompt: What is Partial Pooling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Intermediate between separate and common estimates.
Pooling strength reflects uncertainty and heterogeneity.

cards.definition: No pooling estimates groups independently under the specified model, without a common learned group distribution linking their estimates. It can preserve heterogeneity but yield noisy estimates for sparse groups.
major_error_concepts: Calling a multilevel shrinkage estimate no pooling.
cards.prompt: What is No Pooling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independent group estimation without shared learned pooling.

cards.definition: Complete pooling treats relevant groups as sharing the same parameter, ignoring between-group differences for that component. It can improve precision if the common-parameter assumption is adequate and obscure heterogeneity otherwise.
major_error_concepts: Assuming complete pooling is harmless whenever the total sample size is large.
cards.prompt: What is Complete Pooling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One common parameter across groups.

cards.definition: Shrinkage pulls uncertain estimates toward a common center or regularized region. In hierarchical inference it arises from combining group evidence with the higher-level distribution rather than arbitrarily editing estimates afterward.
major_error_concepts: Treating shrinkage as proof that true group values must be equal.
cards.prompt: What is Shrinkage? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Uncertain estimates move toward the modeled shared distribution.

cards.definition: A centered hierarchical parameterization represents group effects directly as draws from their higher-level distribution. Its sampling geometry can be favorable when group effects are well informed by data and difficult in weak-information funnel-like settings.
major_error_concepts: Assuming centered parameterizations are always computationally superior.
cards.prompt: What is Centered Parameterization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Direct group-effect variables tied to hyperparameters.
Computation depends on data information.

cards.definition: A noncentered parameterization expresses a group effect as a location plus scale times a standardized latent variable. It can reduce posterior coupling in weak-data settings but is not universally better than centered coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Claiming noncentering changes the intended probability model when the transformation is implemented consistently.
cards.prompt: What is Noncentered Parameterization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Standardized latent variable transformed by group location and scale.
Performance depends on information geometry.

accepted_variants: Probabilistic regression with Bayesian parameter updating.
cards.definition: Bayesian regression combines a conditional outcome model with priors over coefficients and other unknowns. Posterior inference and prediction must include the relevant uncertainty rather than only a fitted coefficient vector.
major_error_concepts: Calling any least-squares fit Bayesian without a stated prior model.
cards.prompt: What is Bayesian Regression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Regression likelihood plus priors.
Posterior predictive uncertainty extends beyond coefficient point estimates.

accepted_variants: A prior for residual standard deviation or variance under a declared parameterization.
cards.definition: A noise-scale prior describes uncertainty about residual variability, often constrained to positive values. The choice should be checked on the outcome scale and can strongly affect inference when data are sparse.
major_error_concepts: Using a scale prior that assigns substantial probability to impossible negative standard deviations.
cards.prompt: What is Noise-Scale Prior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Prior on residual scale with appropriate support.
Outcome units and small samples matter.

cards.definition: Bayesian logistic regression models a binary probability through a logistic link applied to predictors and coefficients, with priors on the unknowns. Coefficients act on log odds, not directly as constant changes in probability.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a coefficient of one as a universal one-unit increase in probability.
cards.prompt: What is Bayesian Logistic Regression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Logistic link for binary outcomes.
Coefficients are on the log-odds scale.

cards.definition: In logistic regression with design rows x_i and outcomes y_i, complete separation means some direction v gives (2y_i-1)x_i^T v>0 for every observation. Quasi-complete separation allows all these values to be nonnegative with some strictly positive, while complete separation is absent. Moving coefficients along such a direction prevents a finite likelihood maximum. Near separation can give a finite but unstable estimate. Proper priors give a proper posterior for finite logistic data, but posterior moments and prior sensitivity still need separate attention.
major_error_concepts: Any near separation proves the logistic MLE is infinite, and every proper prior then guarantees a finite posterior coefficient mean.
cards.prompt: Distinguish complete/quasi-complete logistic separation from near separation, and explain what a proper prior does and does not guarantee.
required_concepts: Complete or quasi-complete separation is an exact separating direction, not merely near separation.
The unpenalized likelihood maximum is not attained at finite coefficients in a separating direction.
A proper posterior does not by itself prove precise data identification or finite posterior moments.

cards.definition: A random-intercept model gives groups different baseline levels drawn from a shared distribution. Predictors can share slopes while group intercepts undergo partial pooling.
major_error_concepts: Assuming random intercepts automatically give every group a different slope too.
cards.prompt: What is Random Intercept? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Group-specific baselines with a shared higher-level distribution.

cards.definition: A random-slope model lets predictor effects vary by group through a joint higher-level distribution, often correlated with group intercepts. Appropriate scaling and group information are important for interpreting the variation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all group slope variation is known precisely from one observation per group.
cards.prompt: What is Random Slope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Group-varying predictor coefficients.
Slope and intercept correlations may be modeled.

cards.definition: A predictive target specifies what future quantity and population are being predicted. Prediction for an existing group, a new group, and a changed population can require different integrations and assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Using an existing-group prediction unchanged for an unseen group without integrating new-group uncertainty.
cards.prompt: What is Predictive Target? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Specify future unit, group, and population.
Different targets require different uncertainty treatment.

cards.definition: A posterior predictive check compares observed features with replicated data drawn from the posterior predictive distribution. It probes model adequacy for those features, not whether a posterior computation alone is mathematically correct.
major_error_concepts: Treating one successful check as proof that every aspect of the model is correct.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Predictive Check? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compare data summaries or structure with posterior-predictive replications.
Checks model-data compatibility.

cards.definition: A discrepancy statistic summarizes a feature used to compare observed and replicated data, such as tail behavior, dispersion, or group variation. A check can miss failures in features its discrepancy does not examine.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a mean-only check establishes a correct tail model.
cards.prompt: What is Discrepancy Statistic? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Feature-specific comparison statistic.
Detection scope depends on chosen feature.

cards.definition: Predictive calibration concerns agreement between forecast probabilities and event frequencies under a stated evaluation setting. Calibration alone does not ensure sharp or informative predictions, and the target population matters.
major_error_concepts: Assuming calibrated but extremely diffuse predictions must be useful for every decision.
cards.prompt: What is Predictive Calibration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probability-frequency agreement in the evaluation setting.
Distinct from predictive sharpness.

cards.definition: Simulation-based calibration checks an inference procedure by simulating parameters and data from the model and examining ranks or related posterior diagnostics. It targets computational calibration under that model, not the model's realism for actual data.
major_error_concepts: Claiming successful SBC proves the assumed likelihood is scientifically correct.
cards.prompt: What is Simulation-Based Calibration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Simulate from the assumed joint model and assess posterior ranks or coverage.
Computational check differs from real-world model adequacy.

accepted_variants: An inadequate sampling or structural model.
cards.definition: Model misspecification means the assumed statistical model fails to capture relevant features of the actual data-generating process. A sharply concentrated posterior can still confidently describe an inadequate model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming enough data make every chosen model correct.
cards.prompt: What is Model Misspecification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Relevant mismatch between assumed model and actual process.
Posterior precision is not adequacy.

accepted_variants: Parameter recoverability from the observation model.
cards.definition: A parameter is identifiable when distinct parameter values imply distinguishable observation distributions under the model. Weak identification means data distinguish values only weakly, making prior choices and parameter combinations especially important.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a proper posterior guarantees strong likelihood identification.
cards.prompt: What is Identifiability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distinct parameters induce distinguishable data laws.
Weak identification differs from complete absence of a posterior.

accepted_variants: The mathematical object of posterior computation.
cards.definition: A posterior computation target is the explicitly specified posterior law or expectation to be approximated. An algorithm should be evaluated against that target, not merely by whether it produces plausible-looking numbers.
major_error_concepts: Treating a convenient approximation as the definition of the posterior itself.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Computation Target? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Define the exact distribution or quantity sought.
Separate target from numerical method.

cards.definition: Monte Carlo integration estimates an expectation using averages over random draws from a suitable distribution. Its error decreases statistically under sampling assumptions rather than vanishing simply because a sample looks representative.
major_error_concepts: Assuming finite Monte Carlo output is an exact expectation.
cards.prompt: What is Monte Carlo Integration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Random-sample average approximates an expectation.
Sampling assumptions control error.

cards.definition: Monte Carlo standard error measures numerical uncertainty in an estimated posterior quantity due to finite simulation. It differs from posterior uncertainty about the scientific parameter and depends on dependence among draws.
major_error_concepts: Using posterior standard deviation as the Monte Carlo standard error of its mean without adjustment.
cards.prompt: What is Monte Carlo Error? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Simulation error versus inferential uncertainty.
Autocorrelation affects precision.

cards.definition: Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs dependent draws using a Markov chain designed to have the target posterior as an invariant distribution. Useful estimation also requires adequate exploration and applicable ergodic behavior.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a formally correct transition rule guarantees convergence in a short run.
cards.prompt: What is Markov Chain Monte Carlo? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Dependent chain with target invariant law.
Invariant law alone does not guarantee useful finite sampling.

accepted_variants: An invariant probability law of the chain.
cards.definition: A stationary or invariant distribution is unchanged by one step of a Markov transition kernel. Having the desired invariant distribution is necessary for common MCMC designs but does not by itself establish mixing from an arbitrary start.
major_error_concepts: Equating invariance with independent samples at every step.
cards.prompt: What is Stationary Distribution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Distribution preserved by the transition.
Stationarity differs from rapid convergence.

accepted_variants: Reversibility with respect to the target law.
cards.definition: Detailed balance equates forward and reverse probability flow between states under a distribution and transition kernel. It is a sufficient route to invariance for many MCMC schemes, not a necessary property of every valid sampler.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all valid posterior samplers must satisfy detailed balance.
cards.prompt: What is Detailed Balance? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Pairwise balanced probability flows.
Sufficient for invariance under the standard setting.

cards.definition: At a state x with 0<pi_tilde(x)<infinity, propose y from q(y|x). For an ordinary density-based proposal with q(y|x)>0 and finite target values, accept with alpha(x,y)=min{1, pi_tilde(y)q(x|y)/(pi_tilde(x)q(y|x))}; otherwise retain x. A proposed zero-target state or a move with zero reverse-proposal density is rejected. Target normalization cancels. Detailed balance gives target invariance, but useful convergence and exploration require further chain conditions.
major_error_concepts: Always accept with min(1,pi_tilde(y)/pi_tilde(x)), even if the forward and reverse proposal densities differ.
cards.prompt: Give the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rule, including asymmetric proposals and what invariance alone does not guarantee.
required_concepts: Give the target-times-reverse-proposal over current-target-times-forward-proposal ratio, capped at one.
Keep the current state upon rejection and handle zero numerator as rejection.
Invariance is not by itself a mixing guarantee.

cards.definition: Gibbs sampling updates subsets of variables from their full conditional distributions given the current remaining variables. Easy conditional draws do not guarantee rapid exploration when posterior dependence is strong.
major_error_concepts: Using marginal rather than full conditional distributions and calling it ordinary Gibbs updating.
cards.prompt: What is Gibbs Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sample full conditionals in a specified update scheme.

cards.definition: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo augments continuous parameters with momenta and uses gradient-informed trajectories plus correction to explore a target distribution. It requires suitable differentiable geometry and is not directly an unrestricted sampler for discrete parameters.
major_error_concepts: Assuming numerical trajectory integration has no approximation error needing control.
cards.prompt: What is Hamiltonian Monte Carlo? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Momentum-augmented gradient-informed exploration.
Appropriate differentiability and correction matter.

accepted_variants: Sampler warmup or burn-in, with adaptation explicitly distinguished.
cards.definition: Warmup is an initial simulation phase used to approach typical posterior regions and often adapt algorithm settings. Samples generated during changing adaptation are ordinarily treated differently from retained fixed-kernel inference draws.
major_error_concepts: Assuming deleting a fixed number of early draws proves stationarity.
cards.prompt: What is Warmup? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Initial approach and possible adaptation phase.
Distinguish adaptation samples from retained inference samples.

cards.definition: Autocorrelation measures dependence between chain values separated by a lag. Persistent dependence reduces information about many posterior averages relative to the same number of independent draws.
major_error_concepts: Treating a large raw chain length as equally many independent observations.
cards.prompt: What is Autocorrelation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Lagged dependence within the chain.

cards.definition: Effective sample size estimates how much information a dependent simulation provides for a specified quantity relative to independent draws. It is quantity-dependent and does not certify exploration of undiscovered modes.
major_error_concepts: Using a high ESS for one parameter to prove all posterior tails and modes were explored.
cards.prompt: What is Effective Sample Size? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Independent-draw equivalent for a particular estimand.
Not a universal chain-quality guarantee.

cards.definition: R-hat compares variation within and between multiple chains or split chains to flag lack of agreement. Values near one are useful diagnostics but cannot prove that all chains found every important posterior region.
major_error_concepts: Declaring a posterior fully explored solely because every reported R-hat is close to one.
cards.prompt: What is R-Hat? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Within-between chain comparison.
Near one is not a complete convergence proof.

cards.definition: In Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a divergent transition indicates numerical trajectory behavior that can signal problematic posterior geometry. Such warnings can imply biased exploration and should not be equated with ordinary harmless rejected proposals.
major_error_concepts: Treating divergent transitions as automatically harmless sampling noise.
cards.prompt: What is Divergent Transition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Problematic numerical Hamiltonian trajectory.
May signal exploration bias.

cards.definition: A multimodal posterior has multiple separated regions of high density or probability mass. A chain confined to one mode can give misleadingly precise summaries even when within-mode diagnostics appear good.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a single-mode chain mean as the full posterior expectation without checking mode coverage.
cards.prompt: What is Multimodal Posterior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Multiple separated posterior regions.
Local mixing does not ensure global exploration.

accepted_variants: Weighted posterior integration from a proposal.
cards.definition: Importance sampling draws from a proposal and weights each draw by target density divided by proposal density. The proposal must cover target support, and tail behavior controls weight variance and estimator reliability.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the weight ratio or assuming many draws guarantee finite variance.
cards.prompt: What is Importance Sampling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Target-to-proposal weights.
Support and finite-moment conditions matter.

cards.definition: Self-normalized importance sampling divides weighted sums by the sum of weights, allowing an unnormalized target density. It is generally biased at finite sample size but can be consistent under appropriate conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming self-normalization makes every finite-sample estimator exactly unbiased.
cards.prompt: What is Self-Normalized Weights? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Normalize by total importance weight.
Finite-sample bias can remain.

cards.definition: Variational inference approximates a posterior by optimizing over a chosen family of distributions. Results depend on the family's expressiveness and optimization objective, and uncertainty can be distorted by the approximation.
major_error_concepts: Treating a converged optimization routine as proof of an exact posterior.
cards.prompt: What is Variational Inference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Optimization within an approximate distribution family.
Approximation error remains.

cards.definition: For a variational density q(theta), ELBO(q)=E_q[log p(y,theta)]-E_q[log q(theta)]. With 0<p(y)<infinity and expectations/divergence well-defined, log p(y)=ELBO(q)+KL(q(theta)||p(theta|y)). The nonnegative gap makes this a lower bound. Equality requires q to equal the posterior almost everywhere; a restricted family or an optimizer stopping need not achieve equality.
major_error_concepts: The ELBO gap is KL(posterior||q), and it is zero whenever numerical optimization converges.
cards.prompt: State the ELBO and its exact KL-gap identity, including the direction of KL and equality condition.
required_concepts: State the joint-log-density expectation minus the variational-log-density expectation.
The gap is KL(q||posterior), not the reverse.
Equality requires the actual posterior, not merely optimizer termination.

cards.definition: A Laplace approximation uses a local quadratic expansion of log posterior around a suitable mode to form a Gaussian approximation. It can perform poorly with strong skewness, boundaries, or multiple important modes.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one local Gaussian necessarily captures a multimodal posterior.
cards.prompt: What is Laplace Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Local curvature-based Gaussian approximation.

accepted_variants: The prior predictive density at the observed data.
cards.definition: Marginal likelihood averages fit over the parameter prior, so it rewards data-compatible predictive concentration rather than only the best fit. It can be sensitive to prior width even when posterior parameter estimates are relatively stable.
major_error_concepts: Assuming two models with equal maximum likelihood must have equal evidence.
cards.prompt: What is Marginal-Likelihood Sensitivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Prior-integrated fit.
Prior width can affect model evidence strongly.

accepted_variants: Prior odds among competing model hypotheses.
cards.definition: A prior model probability assigns probability to each candidate model before the current evidence. Posterior model probabilities combine these values with marginal likelihoods; the candidate list itself is part of the assumption.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting model probabilities as covering every conceivable model when only a small list was specified.
cards.prompt: What is Prior Model Probability? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Probability over the stated model set.
Combine with evidence for posterior model weights.

cards.definition: Bayesian model averaging combines predictive distributions or other compatible quantities using posterior model probabilities. It includes uncertainty among the candidate models but not automatically uncertainty about models excluded from the list.
major_error_concepts: Averaging incompatible parameter meanings across models without defining a common target.
cards.prompt: What is Bayesian Model Averaging? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Posterior-weighted model mixture.
Limited to the defined candidate set.

cards.definition: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by evaluating predictions on observations held out from fitting according to a defined split scheme. Dependence, groups, and time ordering must match the intended prediction target.
major_error_concepts: Randomly splitting dependent time-series observations and assuming that estimates future forecasting performance without leakage.
cards.prompt: What is Cross-Validation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Held-out predictive evaluation.
Splits must respect target and dependence.

cards.definition: Leave-one-out predictive evaluation uses each observation's predictive density given all the others. Efficient approximations require their own reliability checks, and leaving out individuals differs from leaving out entire groups.
major_error_concepts: Treating within-group LOO as automatically estimating new-group prediction.
cards.prompt: What is Leave-One-Out Prediction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Predict each held-out unit from the remaining data.
Define the held-out unit appropriately.

cards.definition: For a specified predictive-unit factorization, the variance-penalty version has lppd=sum_i log E_post[p(y_i|theta)] and p_WAIC=sum_i Var_post[log p(y_i|theta)]. Its expected-log-predictive-density estimate is elpd_WAIC=lppd-p_WAIC; the deviance-scale score is WAIC=-2 elpd_WAIC, so smaller is better on that scale. Finite, stably estimated moments and an appropriate predictive-unit definition matter; asymptotic motivation does not guarantee finite-sample accuracy.
major_error_concepts: WAIC is the posterior mean log likelihood plus the variance of the summed log likelihood, with larger values always better under every sign convention.
cards.prompt: State the variance-penalty WAIC formula, declaring its sign convention and predictive-unit assumption.
required_concepts: Use log of the posterior mean likelihood for lppd, not the posterior mean log likelihood.
Subtract the sum of pointwise posterior log-likelihood variances.
Declare the elpd versus minus-two-elpd convention and the relevant predictive units.

accepted_variants: Poor generalization despite strong fitted-data agreement.
cards.definition: Predictive overfitting occurs when a model captures sample-specific variation that fails to generalize to the target data. Priors and partial pooling can reduce it, but a Bayesian label does not eliminate the need for predictive evaluation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming posterior inference automatically prevents every form of overfitting.
cards.prompt: What is Predictive Overfitting? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: In-sample patterns fail out of sample.
Bayesian methods can still overfit.

cards.definition: A prior predictive scale check asks whether draws from the prior and observation model generate plausible data magnitudes and structures. Apparently diffuse parameter priors can imply extreme or concentrated outcomes after nonlinear transformations.
major_error_concepts: Calling a prior uninformative solely because its parameter variance is large.
cards.prompt: What is Prior Predictive Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Assess the implied data distribution, not parameter width alone.

cards.definition: Posterior uncertainty is conditional on the model, data, and prior used. It does not automatically include uncertainty from unmodeled measurement bias, selection mechanisms, or alternative scientific assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Treating one credible interval as a complete account of every possible source of error.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Nature of Posterior Uncertainty? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Posterior is conditional on explicit assumptions.
Omitted uncertainty sources are not automatically covered.

cards.definition: A missing-data model describes how unobserved values and observation indicators relate to the full data. Ignorability depends on assumptions about the missingness mechanism and parameter structure, not simply on the fraction missing.
major_error_concepts: Assuming deleting missing records is unbiased whenever only a small percentage is missing.
cards.prompt: What is Missing-Data Mechanism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Model values and missingness process.
Ignorability requires assumptions.

cards.definition: Censoring retains partial information about a sampled value. For a continuous event time T with CDF F_theta, a fixed right-censoring boundary c gives event T>c and likelihood factor 1-F_theta(c), not the density at c. Fixed interval censoring a<T≤b gives F_theta(b)-F_theta(a). The same simplification requires an ignorable censoring mechanism; if the chance of censoring depends informatively on the unobserved value or target parameters, model that mechanism as part of the observed-data likelihood.
major_error_concepts: A missing event time censored at c always contributes f_theta(c), and any censoring mechanism can be ignored.
cards.prompt: Explain the likelihood contribution of a censored value and the assumption needed to ignore the censoring mechanism.
required_concepts: Censoring records a bound or interval, not an exact value.
Use the matching event probability for fixed or ignorable censoring.
Do not discard an informative observation mechanism.

cards.definition: Truncation excludes observations outside a selection region from the observed sample. The observed-data likelihood must condition on inclusion, unlike censoring where an included observation retains partial information.
major_error_concepts: Treating truncation and censoring as identical likelihood contributions.
cards.prompt: What is Truncation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sampling excludes values outside a region.
Condition the likelihood on selection.

cards.definition: A robust likelihood reduces sensitivity to deviations such as extreme observations, for example through heavier-tailed residual models. It changes the model's assumptions and predictive behavior rather than making all outliers irrelevant.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a heavy-tailed likelihood solves every bias, dependence, or measurement-error problem.
cards.prompt: What is Robust Likelihood? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Likelihood designed for reduced sensitivity to specified deviations.
Robustness is targeted, not universal.

cards.definition: Model sensitivity analysis compares conclusions under plausible alternative likelihoods, structures, or measurement assumptions. It complements prior sensitivity because uncertainty about the sampling model can dominate uncertainty within one posterior.
major_error_concepts: Treating a prior-only sensitivity check as a complete likelihood-model robustness analysis.
cards.prompt: What is Model Sensitivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vary substantive model assumptions, not just priors.

accepted_variants: Prior-averaged risk of a decision procedure.
cards.definition: Bayes risk averages a decision rule's loss over both the prior parameter law and possible data from the sampling model. It evaluates a procedure before the current data, unlike posterior expected loss conditional on observed data.
major_error_concepts: Interchanging Bayes risk and posterior expected loss without the different conditioning.
cards.prompt: What is Bayes Risk? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Average over prior states and possible datasets.
Distinct from posterior loss for one observed sample.

cards.definition: Frequentist coverage is the long-run probability that an interval procedure contains the fixed true parameter under repeated sampling. A credible interval has a different conditional definition and need not have its nominal frequentist coverage in every setting.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every 95 percent credible interval has exact 95 percent coverage for every parameter value.
cards.prompt: What is Frequentist Coverage versus Credibility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Repeated-sampling property of the interval rule.
Different from posterior mass of one realized interval.

cards.definition: Posterior consistency means posterior mass concentrates near the appropriate true parameter or target as information grows under stated conditions. It requires adequate prior support and model or identifiability assumptions and is not guaranteed merely by increasing sample size.
major_error_concepts: Claiming consistency despite a prior excluding every neighborhood of the true parameter.
cards.prompt: What is Posterior Consistency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Asymptotic concentration under explicit assumptions.

accepted_variants: Asymptotic normal posterior approximation under regular conditions.
cards.definition: A Bernstein-von Mises result gives an asymptotically normal posterior with a likelihood-dominated local form in regular finite-dimensional settings. Irregular, boundary, high-dimensional, or nonidentified problems can violate this behavior.
major_error_concepts: Applying likelihood-dominance conclusions to every hierarchical or high-dimensional problem without checking assumptions.
cards.prompt: What is Bernstein–von Mises Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Regular large-sample local normality.
Theorem scope has important exclusions.

accepted_variants: Bayesian updating with a specified sequential sampling mechanism.
cards.definition: Under a fully specified Bayesian model, posterior updating can incorporate sequentially collected evidence without a separate fixed-sample-size formula when the observation and stopping mechanism are appropriately accounted for or ignorable. Predictive calibration and decision performance still depend on those assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any data-dependent selection or stopping process can always be ignored without changing inference.
cards.prompt: What is Sequential Sampling and Stopping? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sequential updating requires an appropriate observation model.
Stopping-rule claims are conditional, not universal.

accepted_variants: The improper-prior boundary for model comparison.
cards.definition: Ordinary Bayes factors require model evidences with meaningful prior normalization. Arbitrary constants in improper priors generally prevent a uniquely defined evidence ratio unless a justified special construction resolves them.
major_error_concepts: Cancelling arbitrary model-specific improper-prior constants without a valid common construction.
cards.prompt: What is Improper Priors and Bayes Factors? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Improper-prior constants can make evidence ratios undefined.
Special alternatives need explicit justification.
